style.summary:
style of A: A is tentative and collaborative, hedging with filler, restating the explanation to check it, and stumbling over some words.
style of B: B is fluent and explanatory, speaking in long technical sentences and answering with short acknowledgments that trail off at the end.

A: A's restatement opens with a check on whether the explanation is right, which lets A set how B's account is framed.
A's checking tone makes B's explanation the thing that has to be confirmed, so A decides what counts as understood.
A keeps speaking after B's brief replies, so the exchange moves in A's direction.
B: B's fluent technical register signals expertise, and A's tentative tone defers to it.
B's long, dense explanation is hard to interrupt, so B keeps the floor for the substance.
B's short Yeah replies accept A's restatement and leave the terms of the explanation with B.

A: Checking one's understanding is a courtesy, and B holds the knowledge and confirms or corrects A's version, so B has the final say.
A's check depends on B's explanation, and B can correct it at any point, so B sets the standard for what counts as understood.
B's brief replies are acknowledgments rather than invitations to continue, and B's earlier explanation shows B driving the topic.
B: Fluency signals expertise, but A's direct questions force B to define terms, so A decides what gets explained.
A long explanation can still be cut in by a question, and A's restatement followed by a new point shows A taking the next turn.
Short acknowledgments of A's restatement are agreement with A's version, so the terms came from A's framing and not from B.

content.summary:
content of A: A asks what combo means, then restates the diagram as features passing through a contextualized layer and a low-pass filter.
content of B: B supplies the technical account of the combo system, with two networks whose outputs are added and passed to a further layer.

A: A's restatement sets out the structure in A's own words, so the working description is A's version.
A's request for a definition puts the topic on the table, which obliges B to explain it.
A's point about the low-pass filter adds a second step to the account that B has to accept.
B: B holds the detailed knowledge of how the combo system is built, which makes B the source of the content.
B's explanation of the two networks and how they are combined sets the technical facts that everything else depends on.
B's account is the one that is correct by construction, so A's restatement has to match it.

A: A's restatement is only a paraphrase of B's account, so the substance stays with B.
A's question is answered by B, who decides how much detail to give, so B controls the depth of the topic.
Accepting a step that B has described does not give A control, because B chose what the step contains.
B: Knowing the detail gives B the answer, but A's restatement shows A can frame that answer in A's own terms.
B's account can be incomplete, and A's restatement exposes the gap, so A can shape which facts get attention.
Being correct does not decide who sets the agenda, and A's restatement is the frame that B is answering.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A holds the floor for most of the turn, opens the restatement, and moves the exchange on to the low-pass filter.
coordination of B: B answers at length and gives brief replies, then stops with an unfinished Yeah so when A continues.

A: A takes the lead by restating the topic and then moves the exchange to a new step.
A decides when the explanation has been understood and moves on, which controls the transition.
A's continued speech after B's short replies gives A most of the talk time.
B: B holds the floor for the long explanation, so B shapes the first part of the exchange.
B's trailing Yeah signals a willingness to let A carry the next part, which keeps B in a supporting role that avoids conflict.
B's responses are timed to A's pauses, so B controls where the turns begin and end.

A: A's movement to a new step depends on B yielding the floor, and B's trailing reply shows B can hold it.
A moves on only after B has finished, so the transition is shaped by B's timing.
Brief replies are acknowledgments, so A's talk time is a consequence of B's choice to stay short.
B: A's restatement is a way to take the floor back, so the long explanation does not last.
Yielding the next part can also mean B has nothing more to add, so B's support is passive.
Timing responses to A's pauses means A's pauses set B's moments to speak, so A controls the rhythm.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A is invested in understanding the design, asking for a definition and checking each step.
engagement of B: B is engaged in explaining, giving a full account, but shows little interest in A's understanding beyond short replies.

A: A's questions show active interest in the design, which draws B into explaining it.
A checks each step of the design, so A shows a sustained commitment to getting it right.
A's restatement invites B to confirm, which keeps A at the centre of the exchange.
B: B's full explanation shows investment in the subject and gives B a central role.
B's knowledge gives B a stake in the design, which others must engage with.
B's short replies keep B out of uncertain territory, so B's position stays secure.

A: A's questions show interest, but B's full answers decide what A learns, so B determines the level of engagement.
Checking each step keeps the design in A's hands only if B accepts the checks, and B can refuse them.
Inviting confirmation makes B the one who approves, so the centre of the exchange is B's to grant.
B: An explanation shows knowledge, but A's questions decide what gets explained, so A has the more active role.
A stake in the design is only useful if the design is accepted, and A's restatement is the version being tested.
Staying in secure territory is a choice that leaves the questions to A, so A determines what is discussed.
